title: Broad Mites
objective: Identify broad mite life stages and characteristic growing-point injury, distinguish Polyphagotarsonemus latus from hemp russet mite, spider mite, herbicide, nutrient, viral, and environmental differentials, and document confirmation at appropriate magnification.

terms.definition: The broad mite, a minute tarsonemid mite with a wide host range that is documented as a pest of indoor Cannabis and hemp.
A family of very small mites that includes broad mite; many species occupy protected young plant tissue and do not produce spider-mite webbing.
Damage concentrated in meristems, expanding leaves, buds, or other young tissue that can cause distortion, hardening, bronzing, stunting, or death of new growth.
An egg with a patterned surface; broad-mite eggs can show distinctive pale bumps or a net-like pattern under sufficient magnification and can support identification.

Transport of one organism by another without parasitizing it; broad-mite dispersal on insects has been documented in other crops and is a general biological mechanism, not a cannabis-specific diagnosis.

coreScience: Broad mite is a microscopic, highly polyphagous mite recognized in greenhouse horticulture and documented as a pest of indoor Cannabis. Adults are much smaller than two-spotted spider mites and typically require at least strong hand-lens magnification or microscopy for reliable observation.

Broad mites tend to occupy young, protected tissues. Feeding is associated with distorted, hardened, bronzed, cupped, twisted, or stunted new growth and malformed buds. Because developing tissues remain deformed after the mites move or decline, visible injury can outlast the active population.

Broad mite does not make the silk webbing typical of two-spotted spider mite. Its injury can overlap strongly with hemp russet mite, cyclamen mite, virus-like symptoms, nutrient disorders including boron or zinc problems, herbicide injury, phytotoxicity, heat or humidity stress, and normal developmental abnormalities. UC IPM specifically warns that broad-mite symptoms resemble adverse growing conditions, nutrient deficiencies, and herbicide injury.

Life-stage morphology can strengthen confirmation. Broad-mite adults are oval and pale; eggs are laid on plant surfaces and can have a characteristic patterned appearance under magnification. Species-level mite identification should be based on specimens rather than the shape of damaged leaves alone.

Cannabis-specific broad-mite research is much thinner than the general greenhouse literature. Published U.S. hemp reviews document the pest association, while most detailed development, temperature, morphology, and management data come from other hosts. Those cross-species mechanisms must be labeled accordingly.
cultivationRelevance: Target scouting at expanding leaves, meristems, buds, and protected folds rather than examining only mature fan leaves.
Photograph new growth serially and pair injury images with direct mite or egg observations so old distortion is not mistaken for continuing population growth.
Use spider-mite webbing, russet-mite body form, organism size, egg morphology, tissue location, and laboratory or expert identification as differential evidence rather than one symptom shortcut.

Separate diagnosis from control selection. Any pesticide or biological-control use must be checked against current crop labels, jurisdictional rules, beneficial-organism compatibility, residue constraints, and production stage.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Record affected meristems, expanding leaves, buds, bronzing, hardening, twisting, cupping, stunting, necrosis, and whether mature tissue is less affected.
Record magnification, adult or immature body form, approximate size, color, egg appearance, protected-site location, and identifier confidence.
Record webbing presence/absence, russet-mite search, nutrition/root-zone data, chemical exposure history, environmental events, and infectious-disease evidence.
Map propagation lot, plant-to-plant clustering, growing-point severity, incoming material, handling sequence, and spread over time.
After a supported correction or population decline, record whether subsequently formed tissue develops normally; do not expect already deformed tissue to become normal.

misconceptions: Twisted new growth is specific for broad mite.
Broad mites produce the same obvious webbing as two-spotted spider mites.
Old distorted leaves prove broad mites are still active.
A cannabis-specific broad-mite temperature or action threshold has been universally validated.
A low-magnification symptom inspection is equivalent to specimen identification.
evidenceLimits: Broad mite is documented on Cannabis, but the most detailed morphology, life-history, and environmental-response literature is derived from other greenhouse crops. Those mechanisms can guide identification while remaining cross-species evidence. Cannabis-specific economic thresholds, cultivar susceptibility, and treatment performance are not sufficiently standardized to support universal action numbers.
